title: Teams and accounts
standfirst: Organisations, key scopes, spend limits, SSO, audit and residency. The features a team needs are rarely the ones a solo builder notices, and several providers only sell them on an enterprise tier.
idea: A sandbox account is a billing boundary, a permission boundary and sometimes a data boundary. The first question is what the account owns: keys, wallet, machines, snapshots. The second is who can see and spend what.

Spend controls come in three strengths. A hard cap stops machines when reached. A per-key or per-project limit blocks one credential. An alert tells you after the fact. Providers differ on which they offer, and several offer none.

Audit and residency are the enterprise questions. A lifecycle activity log is not a compliance audit log. A compute region is not a data-residency guarantee if backups and control-plane records sit elsewhere.

splits.heading: Organisations are usually shared wallets
body: Sandboxer's organisation is a shared wallet with per-seat pricing; boxd's account is an organisation with owner, admin and member roles; Boat and Agent 37 have workspaces that own keys, wallet and machines. E2B separates a workspace, which shares payment and credits, from projects, which have their own plans and spending limits.
The consequence is that a per-seat plan multiplies. A five-person team on Sandboxer's $20 plan pays $100 a month before usage.

splits.heading: Hard caps are rarer than alerts
body: Runtime caps spend per key per day and per sandbox over its life. InstaBox has a monthly cap that stops machines. Agent 37 has per-instance budget ceilings, which are not money. Vercel offers spend management that can pause projects.
Lizard says plainly that there is no spending cap, and boxd publishes no budget or alert feature at all. Boat has no dollar cap on a personal account.

splits.heading: SSO, audit and residency
body: Runtime includes SSO, SCIM and a 400-day audit log free. InstaBox and Lizard put SSO and audit on Enterprise. Vercel sells SAML at $300 a month. Agent 37, Boat, boxd, Sandboxer and Sprites publish no SSO or audit log on the tiers described here.
Residency is separate. Boat and boxd are EU-only. Agent 37 keeps compute in the chosen region but stores backups in the US. InstaBox and Runtime are US-only.

watchFor: Whether the plan price multiplies per seat.
Whether there is a hard spend cap, a per-key limit, or only an alert.
Whether SSO and audit logs are included, enterprise-only, or absent.
Whether backups and control-plane data sit in the same region as compute.
Whether an API key can be scoped to one sandbox or one project.

rows.scenario: Per-instance budget ceilings stop a runaway instance, but they are not a money cap; no audit log or SSO is published.
rows.note: Workspaces own keys, wallet and instances; teams have admin and user roles; each instance has a budget ceiling. No audit log or SSO is published, and backups are stored in the US.

source.quote: A workspace is the account: it owns the API keys, the wallet, and every instance.

rows.scenario: Admin, member and viewer roles with scoped service accounts; no hard spend cap is published and SAML needs a feature flag.
rows.note: Workspace roles are admin, member and viewer; service accounts have scoped tokens; SAML and directory sync require a feature flag. No hard spend cap or full audit coverage is published.

source.quote: There are three roles that a user or service account can have in a workspace

rows.scenario: Owner, admin and member roles and per-member caps, but start budgets are pooled and there is no audit log or SSO.
rows.note: Organisations with owner, admin and member roles, scoped keys and per-member caps. No audit log or SSO is published, and start budgets are pooled across the organisation.

source.quote: The included time, start-rate and concurrency numbers of the plan are **one shared pool for the whole organization**.

rows.scenario: Owner, admin and member roles with keys fenced to one org; no self-serve audit log, SSO or spend cap is published.
rows.note: Every account is an organisation with owner, admin and member roles, and keys are fenced to one org. No self-serve audit log, SSO or spend cap is published; machines are EU-only.

source.quote: Every account is an organization.

rows.scenario: Budget alerts email you after the loop; they do not pause or cap anything, and the account ceiling is 1,500 concurrent vCPU.
rows.note: Budget alerts are informational and do not cap usage. Concurrency is account-wide: 1,500 vCPU, 6 TiB and 30 TB. No per-sandbox IAM; the account audit log records control-plane actions only.

source.quote: Budget alerts are informational only. They do not pause or cap usage.

rows.scenario: The runaway agent is capped only by the prepaid pool, and every member of the organisation can exec in every running sandbox.
rows.note: Tiers are prepaid top-ups that set an org-wide vCPU, memory and disk pool. Any member or API key can address any running sandbox. SSO is Enterprise; audit logs are role-gated and export is coming soon.

source.quote: Every member of an organization can address that organization's running sandboxes

rows.scenario: The workspace shares payment and credits while each project has its own spending limit; SSO and audit coverage are not published.
rows.note: A workspace shares payment, credits and invoice; each project has its own plan and spending limit. SOC 2 Type II and a HIPAA BAA path. SSO and audit coverage are not published.

source.quote: When a project reaches its spending limit, only that project is blocked.

rows.scenario: A monthly spend cap stops machines; SSO, SCIM and audit logs are Enterprise only.
rows.note: Organisations and workspaces with roles, scoped keys and a monthly spend cap that stops machines. SSO, SCIM and audit logs are Enterprise only.

source.quote: caps this month's usage beyond the org's allowance

rows.scenario: Caps on sandboxes, CPU, memory and disk, but no spending cap at all; SSO and audit are Enterprise.
rows.note: Workspaces, projects and scoped keys, with caps on sandboxes, CPU, memory and disk. No spending cap at all; SSO and audit logs are Enterprise only.

source.quote: A scoped key works only inside its projects or workspaces.

rows.scenario: An environment budget on Team stops the workload at the limit; Starter has no budgets and only three seats.
rows.note: Environment budgets on Team and Enterprise stop workloads at the limit. RBAC is Team+, SSO and audit logs are Enterprise. Starter has 3 seats and 100 containers.

source.quote: When the spend limit is reached, Modal stops workloads that would incur additional out-of-pocket charges.

rows.scenario: Devboxes are shareable inside the organisation and an SSH-key audit endpoint exists; SSO and hard caps are not published.
rows.note: Devboxes are shareable to anyone in the organisation, and an SSH-key audit endpoint exists. SSO, hard spend caps and comprehensive audit coverage are not published.

source.quote: devboxes are shareable live via URL to anyone in your Morph Cloud organization

rows.scenario: Per-key daily spend limits and a per-sandbox lifetime cap, with SSO, SCIM and a 400-day audit log free.
rows.note: Roles, compartments that wall off key groups, per-key daily spend limits and a per-sandbox lifetime cap. SSO, SCIM and a 400-day audit log are free.

source.quote: read-only keys, a daily spending limit per key, and compartments

rows.scenario: A shared wallet with per-member usage caps; plans are per seat and no audit log or SSO is published.
rows.note: An organisation is a shared wallet with owner and member roles, scoped keys and per-member usage caps. Plans are per seat, and no audit log or SSO is published.

source.quote: An **organization** is a shared wallet: one plan, one balance, and the members who run sandboxes on it.

rows.scenario: Fly organisations and connector management; spend caps, key scopes and audit retention are not published.
rows.note: Fly.io organisations and connector management in a dashboard. SSO is claimed by a third party; spend caps, key scopes, audit retention and residency are not published.

source.quote: Sprites uses your Fly.io account for authentication

rows.scenario: Spend management can pause projects and SAML costs $300 a month; fine-grained Sandbox key scopes are not published.
rows.note: Team seats, spend management that can pause projects, and a lifecycle activity log. SAML costs $300 a month; fine-grained Sandbox key scopes and contractual residency are not published.

source.quote: SAML Single Sign-On: $300/month

rows.scenario: Organisations and projects with admin and member roles and project-scoped keys; no budget is published, so a runaway loop is stopped only by an empty credit balance.
rows.note: Org admin and member roles, project admin and member roles, and API keys limited to project-member permissions. SSO over OIDC or SAML is available to org admins but has to be enabled for the organisation. No spend cap, budget alert or audit-log product is published; prepaid credits are the stop, and Pro adds a 1,000-sandbox concurrency ceiling.

source.quote: When the balance reaches zero, Tensorlake blocks new sandbox activity and stops running sandboxes instead of creating a postpaid overage.

rows.scenario: A team shares Droplets and billing, with roles and OIDC single sign-on, but a spend alert cannot stop the bill.
rows.note: Six predefined roles plus custom roles, OIDC single sign-on, and spend alerts at percentage thresholds of a budget. The docs say a budget is not a cap; the only pause exists for model access key alerts. Account-wide audit logs are not published for Droplets.

source.quote: A spend alert budget is not a spending cap and does not limit how much you can use, unless you enable pausing on a model access key alert.

rows.scenario: Five developers share a project with roles and read-only API keys; the bill is the owner's, and nothing stops a runaway machine.
rows.note: Projects with Owner, Admin, Member and Restricted roles, per-project API tokens and cost alerts. No SSO is documented, there is no account audit log with user attribution, and there is no hard spending cap: alerts only send email and never stop a machine.

source.quote: These alerts are optional and are meant to help you keep track of your spending. They are a convenience feature rather than a spending limit

rows.figure: 2 roles; no SSO or spend cap
rows.scenario: Five people share the VPS through Account Sharing; one runaway agent cannot be stopped by an account-level spend cap.
rows.note: Account Sharing gives a collaborator access to selected services with a Collaborator or Admin role. There is no SSO, no account-wide spend cap and no full audit log; the VPS API keeps an action log and the account shows sign-ins.

source.quote: you choose a role for the shared user: Collaborator or Admin

rows.scenario: Add a developer: create a team identity, grant one VM and one Linux user, and hand over a scoped token.
rows.note: Teams, per-VM identities and tokens exist. Named roles, a dollar spend cap and usage alerts are not documented; SAML SSO, SCIM and audit logs are Enterprise-only.

source.quote: Freestyle identities let an end user or agent operate an existing VM without receiving your team API key.

rows.scenario: A small team can share the account with per-service permissions and an audit trail, but there is no SSO and no hard spend cap.
rows.note: The owner can add colleagues as users with their own sign-in and choose which services, domains, invoices, tickets and orders each may see, or invite an agency through delegated access. An audit log keeps 90 days of account changes with CSV export, and six second factors are available. What is missing for a company: SAML/SSO (sign-in is BankID, Google or email plus password), scoped roles beyond per-service visibility, and any hard cap on spend — Cost Management alerts but does not stop a purchase.

source.quote: Invite colleagues to the account with granular permissions instead of sharing login credentials.

scenario.title: Five people, one runaway agent, one procurement form
scenario.setup: A five-person team shares an account. On Tuesday night an agent loops and burns $400 of compute. The same week, procurement asks for SSO and an audit log.

beats.what: The loop starts. A hard cap stops the machine; an alert tells you at 08:00.
You read the bill. Whether the plan multiplies per seat decides what the other four people cost.
Procurement asks who signed in, what they did, and whether the account supports SAML.

scenario.turn: Hard caps are rarer than alerts, and audit logs are rarer than SSO. Runtime is the outlier that includes both free; several providers publish neither on the tiers described here.

questions: Does the plan price multiply per seat, and what does a five-person team pay before usage?
Is there a hard spend cap that stops machines, a per-key limit, or only an alert?
Are SSO and audit logs included, enterprise-only, or absent — and how long is the audit log retained?
Do backups and control-plane data sit in the same region as compute?
Can an API key be scoped to one sandbox or one project, and who can see the wallet?
